criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and resident experiences of extreme water supply shortages, intermittent piped water connections from KUKL, and reliance on public taps, private wells, and informal water tankers/vendors in the Kathmandu Valley, Nepal.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 but fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper includes 'Water governance' as a keyword and empirically captures resident perceptions of government incapacity, delays in the PPP-led Melamchi Water Supply Project, politicized staffing and corruption in the public water utility (KUKL), municipal billing despite poor supply, and unregulated informal water markets (Themes 3 and 5). Under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type clarification, however, the study fails Criterion 2: its primary analytical focus is psychological and cognitive coping narratives ('emotional numbing' vs. 'rational calculus of trade-offs' in constructing a 'fabula of resilience'), and the institutional elements discussed are generic infrastructure project delivery delays (the Melamchi tunnel project) and broad perceptions of macro-governance failure/corruption rather than a specific rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household service access (such as eligibility rules, documentation/tenure requirements, tariff rules, or enforcement).
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative empirical study using a phenomenological hermeneutical ('lived experiences') approach based on primary interviews with 55 Kathmandu residents across two rounds between May and July 2016 (including 36 in-depth 60-minute interviews transcribed, translated, and coded in NVivo).
criterion_notes.c4: Although the primary theoretical outcome is psychological/social resilience and public inaction ('fabula of resilience'), the qualitative data directly report household water access outcomes including severe intermittency/unreliability of piped supply (e.g., receiving water once a week, once in 10 days, or not at all for a month despite a piped connection), time/queuing burdens at public taps, and affordability burdens/coping expenditures on tanker and bottled water.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (individual adult residents of households in Kathmandu, Nepal; n=55 total, n=36 in-depth interviews), study exposure/context (chronic municipal water shortage and delayed Melamchi Water Supply Project delivery), outcomes (self-perceived resilience/coping narratives alongside reported water supply intermittency and coping expenditures), and study design (qualitative phenomenological interview study) are all clearly identifiable, though the exposure is outside the narrow rule-type scope.

evidence_quotes.quote: This paper sheds light on such phenomena by constructing a fabula (or narrative structure) of the paradox by investigating the case of extreme water shortage and the coping strategies of residents in the Kathmandu Valley, Nepal.

Using a lived experiences approach, we investigate the subjective narratives of the delayed project; in particular, the self-reported perceptions of the residents’ resilience or ability to cope with adversity which engenders the self-perception of resilience, so as to identify the extent to which these two hypotheses hold true in the case of Kathmandu.
At the same time, there are no legal or institutional mechanisms that regulate the price, quantity, or quality of water sold by these vendors (Moench, 2001).

Based on the first round of interviews, a detailed set of questions were prepared and a subsequent interview session was carried out in the month of July 2016. A total of 36 local residents of Kathmandu were interviewed.
Participants are often acutely aware of the monetary cost of obtaining bottled and tanked water when piped water supply becomes intermittent, citing figures and comparing costs with household income.

raw_response.exposure: Chronic municipal water scarcity, delays in the Melamchi Water Supply Project, and perceived incapacity/corruption of the government and water utility (KUKL)
raw_response.outcome: Psychological/narrative 'paradox of resilience' (emotional numbing vs. rational calculus of trade-offs) alongside household coping strategies, intermittent piped water availability, and expenditures on informal tanker/bottled water
raw_response.population_and_sample: Local adult residents of Kathmandu, Nepal (55 respondents across two interview rounds in May–July 2016, including 36 in-depth interviewees aged 26–75 coded in NVivo)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. This qualitative phenomenological study investigates how Kathmandu residents construct narratives of coping and 'social resilience' (testing psychological hypotheses of emotional numbing vs. rational trade-off calculus) amid chronic water shortages and delays in the Melamchi Water Supply Project. While respondents discuss distrust in government capacity, corruption/mismanagement in the water utility (KUKL), and reliance on unregulated private water vendors—which would satisfy a broad/plain reading of Criterion 2 ('governance/institutional factor')—the study does not empirically examine any specific legal, regulatory, or administrative rule-type mechanism governing household water access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation rules, tariff structures, or disconnection/enforcement rules), focusing instead on psychological adaptation to infrastructure project delays and general macro-governance failure.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative phenomenological hermeneutical interview study ('lived experiences' approach coded with NVivo)
